analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and pays for it by taxing income above $250,000 and investment gains.
analysis.headline: The bill expanded Social Security benefits and raised the taxes to pay for them, but no other senator signed on and the Senate Finance Committee never took it up before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise Social Security benefits by up to 15% for all beneficiaries, switch the annual cost-of-living adjustment to a measure of prices seniors actually face, and guarantee a minimum benefit at least at the poverty line for people who worked many years at low wages. To pay for it, it would apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $250,000 (they currently stop around $118,500) and raise the tax on investment income from 3.8% to 10%. The bill was introduced by one senator, never got a single cosponsor, and the Finance Committee, to which it was referred, took no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries: everyone would get an across-the-board increase reaching 15% by 2035, annual cost-of-living adjustments would track the spending patterns of elderly households, and lifetime low earners with long work histories would be guaranteed a benefit tied to the poverty line. The higher taxes fall on households earning above $250,000 in wages and on people with significant investment income.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: Raises every beneficiary's primary insurance amount by 1% per year starting in 2021, reaching a 15% increase in 2035 and beyond.

Changes the cost-of-living adjustment from the standard Consumer Price Index to the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers, which reflects what seniors actually buy, and directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish that index monthly.

Sets a new minimum benefit for lifetime low earners: someone with 26 or more years of work would be guaranteed at least a poverty-level benefit, with smaller guarantees scaled down to 6.25% of that amount at 11 years of work, and the change applies to existing beneficiaries through recomputation.
Pays for the expansion by applying Social Security payroll and self-employment taxes to wages above $250,000, which are currently exempt above the contribution and benefit base, effective after 2015.
Raises the net investment income tax from 3.8% to 10%, directing 62% of the proceeds to the Social Security trust fund and 9% to the disability trust fund.

analysis.who_pays: High-income households: employees and self-employed people with wages or earnings above $250,000 would pay Social Security taxes on the excess, and taxpayers with substantial investment income would pay a 10% tax on it instead of 3.8%. Social Security beneficiaries with high incomes would also receive the same across-the-board increase as everyone else.

drawbacks.text: The across-the-board benefit increase is not means-tested: wealthy retirees receive the same 15% boost as low earners, which is a costly way to target help at seniors who need it most.

The bill significantly raises taxes on high earners and on investment income, and its sponsor did not attract a single cosponsor from either party, suggesting broad resistance to the tax side of the package.

Using the Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers would generally produce somewhat larger annual adjustments than the current index, adding to the program's long-term cost even as the new taxes are meant to cover it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and progressive at the bottom: a poverty-level minimum benefit for long-career low earners is a direct anti-poverty measure, and a senior-specific price index better matches seniors' real costs. The cost side is a substantial, explicit tax increase on high wages and investment income, which is why the bill found no co-sponsors; the untargeted across-the-board increase is the weakest part of the design because it sends the largest checks to the best-off retirees.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until that Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sanders introduced the bill on March 12, 2015, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The bill had zero cosponsors, so no other senator put their name on it.
The Finance Committee took no further action; the congressional record shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households earning above $250,000 and taxpayers with large investment income are better off, since the payroll and investment tax increases never took effect; the Finance Committee and Senate leadership never had to take a position on the record. Social Security beneficiaries, especially lifetime low earners, are worse off than they would have been under the bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners and investors who avoided the new taxes

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Social Security Expansion Act and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No partisan vote ever occurred; the bill had a single Independent sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill would tax wages above $250,000 and nearly triple the tax on investment income (3.8% to 10%) to fund benefit increases. Its failure left those tax obligations off the books. The industry's financial interest (keeping the lower rates) runs directly against the bill's benefit expansions for seniors.
Self-employment earnings above $250,000 would become subject to Social Security tax, ending an exemption above the wage base. High-earning self-employed people gained from the bill never advancing.
